study_identification_part.si3_author_journal_year: Oliveira-Saraiva and Ferreira, Frontiers in Psychiatry, 2023
study_identification_part.si4_title: Normative model detects abnormal functional connectivity in psychiatric disorders

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: To develop and evaluate a normative model based on autoencoders trained on resting-state functional MRI data from healthy controls to quantify individual deviations and identify abnormal functional brain network connectivity patterns in schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder.

rci7_preprocessing_pipeline.supporting_text: brain extraction of the T1-weighted images of all subjects was performed with the OASIS template using the Advanced Normalization Tools (ANTs)... the pre-processing of rs-fMRI images was handled within the FMRIB Software Library (FSL)... motion correction using the MCFLIRT tool... spatial smoothing using a Gaussian kernel with 5 mm full width at half maximum (FWHM)... highpass filter with a cut-off of 0.01 Hz... single-session spatial independent component analysis (ICA)... the FSL's tool FMRIB's ICA-based Xnoiseifier (FIX) was applied to automatically detect and remove non-brain signal components... FSL FIX was used for automatic detection and removal of non-brain signal ICA components after hand-labeling training on 10 subjects per dataset.

nm1_model_origin.supporting_text: Autoencoder was the selected architecture for the generation of the normative model, and it was implemented using the Keras Python library.

nm2_modeling_method.reason: The study explicitly uses an autoencoder architecture for normative modeling. The autoencoder learns to reconstruct healthy functional connectivity patterns and identifies deviations in patient data through reconstruction error.
nm2_modeling_method.supporting_text: Here, we propose a normative model based on autoencoders... The underlying concept is that the autoencoder learns to copy the input data to its output. Therefore, the proposed autoencoder will learn to encode the healthy patterns from the input data to the latent representation, and then, only using the information from the latent representation, will try to reconstruct the input data as closely as possible to the original input data. As such, when presented with patient data it is expected that the reconstruction 'fails,' and therefore abnormal functional connectivity patterns can be identified.

nm3_software_tool.reason: The autoencoder implementation is explicitly stated to use the Keras Python library.
nm3_software_tool.supporting_text: Autoencoder was the selected architecture for the generation of the normative model, and it was implemented using the Keras Python library.

nm4_response_variable.answer: Functional connectivity: Pearson correlation coefficients between 14 functional brain network time series (91 unique pairs from 14×14 correlation matrix, lower triangular without diagonal)
nm4_response_variable.reason: The response variable is clearly defined as functional connectivity measured by Pearson correlations between 14 functional brain networks. The 14×14 matrix yields 91 unique features after removing redundancy.
nm4_response_variable.supporting_text: The Pearson's correlation coefficients between the time series of all FBNs pairs were calculated. In the end, a 14 × 14 functional connectivity matrix was created for each subject, giving information about inter FBNs connectivity. Considering that Pearson's correlation coefficient has no information about the direction of functional connectivity, the network matrix is symmetric. Therefore, to avoid redundancy, the diagonal matrix and one-half of the network matrix were discarded. Taking into account that 14 × 14 - 14 / 2 = 91, the remaining half of the matrix was transformed into a vector containing 91 features (pairs of FBNs) for feeding the normative model.

caa6_deviation_metric.answer: Mean squared error per subject (MSEs): reconstruction error between autoencoder output and input; Mean squared error per feature (MSEf): reconstruction error for each FBN pair; Binarized abnormal pairs using top 20% threshold (threshold=1); Graph-theoretic node degree: number of abnormal connections per FBN; Absolute difference between reconstructed and input features for individual-level analysis
caa6_deviation_metric.reason: The paper clearly describes multiple deviation metrics used at different levels of analysis: subject-level (MSEs), feature-level (MSEf), binarized matrices with threshold, and graph theory metrics (node degree).
caa6_deviation_metric.supporting_text: a global metric per subject was defined by calculating the mean squared error between the reconstructed data and the input data of the autoencoder for each subject of the different sets (MSEs)... The generated difference vectors for each subject were reshaped into a 14 × 14 lower triangular matrix, and binarized using the threshold that is defined in the results section. Note that the retained values represent pairs of FBNs that were more abnormal. Graph theory was used to obtain the network degree for each subject... To study which pairs of FBNs were abnormal in each test set, the mean squared error was calculated for each feature, giving a global metric per feature [mean squared error per feature (MSEf)]... For defining the threshold, we first merged the difference vectors of all subjects used to test the autoencoder. Then, we considered the 20% higher values of the merged vector, which corresponds to a threshold value equal to 1.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Mann-Whitney tests compared MSEs distributions between patient groups and healthy controls, and between different patient groups (p=0.05). Graph theory analysis compared median node degree distributions across groups and for individual FBNs. MSEf matrices were generated for each group and differences (patient MSEf minus healthy MSEf) were calculated to identify disorder-specific abnormal FBN pairs. The 10% worst reconstructed pairs were identified for characterization of each disorder. Individual-level analysis examined absolute reconstruction error patterns for characteristic FBN pairs to assess heterogeneity within groups. Additional robustness analysis doubled H-Test-U size (78 subjects) with corresponding H-Train reduction (327 subjects) to validate findings.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: The autoencoder-based normative model successfully identified disorder-characteristic functional connectivity patterns agreeing with literature, and generalized to an independent SCZ dataset (COBRE), but group-level differences did not withstand individual-level analysis, revealing high heterogeneity within psychiatric disorders.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: Patients showed significantly higher reconstruction errors than healthy controls (Mann-Whitney p<0.05 for all comparisons: H-Test-U vs SCZ-Test-U p=0.002, vs BD-Test-U p=0.011, vs ADHD-Test-U p=0.007), but patient groups did not differ significantly from each other (p>0.3). Basal ganglia network (BGN) connectivity plays an important role in BD and SCZ, with BGN-language network connectivity more specific to BD. In SCZ, connections involving higher visual network (HVN) and right executive control network (RECN), particularly HVN-RECN and ASN-BGN pairs, were most relevant. In ADHD, anterior salience network (ASN)-precuneus network (PN) connectivity was most relevant. Characteristic SCZ pairs included ASN-BGN, BGN-HVN, HVN-RECN, ASN-LECN, BGN-PSN, and HVN-PVN. BD was characterized by BGN-DDMN, BGN-HVN, BGN-LN, HVN-PVN, AN-BGN, AN-PVN, and PVN-RECN. ADHD showed abnormalities in ASN-LN, ASN-PN, LN-RECN, HVN-PVN, ASN-VN, and LN-VN. Independent validation on COBRE showed similar patterns for SCZ groups (6 of 9 thresholded pairs shared: ASN-BGN, BGN-HVN, BGN-DDMN, ASN-LN, LN-SN, PN-VDMN), supporting generalizability. However, individual-level analysis revealed high heterogeneity within each patient group, with reconstruction error patterns varying substantially across individuals despite group-level trends, suggesting psychiatric disorders exist on a continuous spectrum with undefined boundaries.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: The study demonstrates that unsupervised deep learning normative modeling can identify functional connectivity patterns characterizing psychiatric disorders without requiring diagnostic labels during training. The approach allows localization of abnormalities at the network-pair level. The findings support a precision-based medical approach focused on individual-level functional network changes rather than traditional group-based diagnostic classification. The authors suggest future work should incorporate unsupervised clustering following normative modeling to identify subgroups within psychiatric disorders. The model's architecture consisted of three hidden layers (91-46-13-46-91), leaky ReLU activation, L2 regularization (1e-5), dropout (0.5), MSE loss, He initialization, trained for 1,000 epochs with Adam optimizer (β1=0.9, β2=0.999, ε=1e-7, learning rate=0.0005). Standardization used only H-Train statistics to avoid data leakage.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: No handling of nuisance structure (site, scanner, age, sex effects) beyond preprocessing; short scan durations and limited temporal resolution; template for dual regression not specific to study data; intranetwork connectivity not explored; small sample sizes; autoencoder did not incorporate age/sex information; medication doses, disease severity, and disease course not controlled; functional connectivity may be less stable than structural measures; some pairs of FBNs that were poorly reconstructed for healthy controls may represent natural variability rather than pathology, potentially limiting model specificity.

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: CoRR healthy subsets included: BNU3 (48), HNU1 (30), IPCAS1 (30), IPCAS3 (34), IPCAS4 (20), MRN1 (39), NYU2 (81), Utah1 (16), Utah2 (1), totaling 299 subjects from CoRR. Combined with UCLA healthy subjects (67 based on original sample before splitting), the training pool was 366. The 14 functional brain networks (FBNs) analyzed were from Shirer et al. template: anterior salience network (ASN), auditory network (AN), basal ganglia network (BGN), dorsal default mode network (DDMN), higher visual network (HVN), language network (LN), left executive control network (LECN), posterior salience network (PSN), precuneus network (PN), primary visual network (PVN), right executive control network (RECN), sensorimotor network (SN), ventral default mode network (VDMN), and visuospatial network (VN). Original sample was 700 subjects, reduced from larger initial dataset by applying inclusion criteria (age 18-50 years, TR=2s, eyes open during scan). After QC exclusions (32 subjects for motion, additional subjects for missing data), final sample was 655 subjects. The study notes comparison difficulties between COBRE and UCLA healthy groups (H-Test-C vs H-Test-U Mann-Whitney p=0.1), suggesting dataset-specific patterns. An additional robustness analysis doubled H-Test-U to 78 subjects (correspondingly reducing H-Train to 327) to validate which FBN pairs consistently characterize each disorder. Acquisition parameters varied across sites (Table 1): scanners included Siemens TrioTim, GE Discovery MR750, Siemens Allegra; field strength all 3T; TE ranged 15-30ms; acquisition time 5:04-10:00 min; time points 150-300; voxel sizes 3-4mm isotropic. Eyes-open condition varied: 1=fixated on target, 2=toward blank screen, 3=open (unspecified).
